paras: The shooting at William Ford took place in Martinsburg, West Virginia, on the evening of Monday, August 20, 1900, when Policeman Dutrow fired at Ford, a Black transfer-wagon driver, as he fled arrest on a warrant. The shot missed, and Ford was caught after a street chase in which a crowd joined and stones were reportedly thrown at him. The local paper wrote that a "general race riot" had been feared.
The warrant stemmed from a Friday-night quarrel over a baseball game between Ford and Arthur Fisher at Randolph Ramer's restaurant.

According to the Martinsburg Herald, Dutrow found Ford on East Martin street shortly after seven, and Ford ran while the officer was reading him the warrant. With Chief of Police Freeze and his dog also in pursuit, Dutrow, "a good distance behind him," fired down Queen street; bystanders said the bullet struck the People's Bank building. Dutrow continued the chase in a buggy, and a "yelling and whooping" crowd joined in; it was "said" that Ford had to dodge stones thrown on Water street "by people endeavoring to stop him." Dutrow caught him in Jacob Custer's yard on East John street, held him at gunpoint and handcuffed him; on the way to the lock-up, the paper said, Ford shoved the officer into the street.

The Herald described Black residents angry that the officer had fired at his prisoner and white onlookers "indignant" at Ford's resistance, but said the street was calm again within about an hour. No report of a hearing or penalty for Ford, or of any inquiry into the shooting, appears in the coverage.

The Herald ran the story on August 25 under the headline "A LIVELY TIME. Officer Dutrow Has a Long Chase. Fires Down Main Street." Its tone was jocular (the bullet went "singing a merry tune" past Ford), and it called Ford "the originator of the trouble." It told the story from the officer's side while recording Black anger at the shooting. It paired the chase with "another provoking incident" that evening, an assault by Frank "Chub" Sampson, described as colored, on D. H. Baker, "a young man from the country." No wire report, other white paper or Black-press account was found.

reader.title: Shooting at William Ford in Martinsburg
bases: A city policeman fired at a fleeing Black man he was trying to arrest on a warrant and later held him at gunpoint; no mob attack or killing is reported (A1).
Only the local Martinsburg Herald reported the chase and shooting; no wire story, other white paper or Black-press account was found (A1).

accounts.label: Local white paper (officer's side)
accounts.gist: Ford ran while Dutrow was reading him the warrant; Dutrow fired from 'a good distance behind' and missed, chased him with a crowd that reportedly stoned him, caught him at gunpoint, and Ford shoved the officer on the way to the lock-up.

framing.detail: The Martinsburg Herald headlined it 'A LIVELY TIME. Officer Dutrow Has a Long Chase. Fires Down Main Street,' told the chase as comedy, blamed Ford as 'the originator of the trouble' and stressed Black anger and white indignation, while noting the colored population was enraged by the shooting.

sources.note: Only report found: local account 'A LIVELY TIME' of Officer Dutrow firing at William Ford during a chase on a warrant, a stone-throwing crowd, the arrest, and fears of a 'race riot'; also reports an unrelated assault by Frank 'Chub' Sampson the same evening.
quotes: the somewhat unusual sight of a negro running down Main street followed by a blue-coat and a bullet
The colored population was enraged at the act of the officer in firing at his intended prisoner
It would have taken the slightest provocation to fan the sparks of anger into flames of conflict, resulting in a general race riot.
When the fleeing man was about the middle of the square Officer Dutrow, who was a good distance behind him, pulled his gun and fired.
It is said that the fleeing man had to dodge a number of stones thrown at him on Water street by people endeavoring to stop him.
